input.question: The Hubble Deep Field shoes thousands of galaxies from soon after the Big Bang. How is it we see these galaxies in every direction of the sky if the universe has expanded so much? Shouldn't they all be centred near one place in the sky? (i.e. near the Big Bang)
input.ground_truth: The Big Bang was not an event which happened in a particular location. It happened everywhere at once, and "everywhere" was a lot closer together at the time. The expansion is that everywhere is becoming more distant from everywhere else, not that things are hurtling away from some central point.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: The Hubble Deep Field shoes thousands of galaxies from soon after the Big Bang. How is it we see these galaxies in every direction of the sky if the universe has expanded so much? Shouldn't they all be centred near one place in the sky? (i.e. near the Big Bang)

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a really, really big balloon. You draw a bunch of dots (these are like galaxies) all over the balloon with a marker. Now, you blow up the balloon really big. What happens to the dots?

At first, the dots are close together. But as you blow up the balloon, the dots spread out and get farther apart. Now, if you look from any spot on the balloon, you can see lots of dots all around you—not just in one spot. They’re everywhere!

The universe is kind of like that big balloon. After the Big Bang, everything started in one tiny spot. But as the universe grew (like the balloon getting bigger), all the galaxies spread out in every direction. So now, no matter where you look in the sky, you see galaxies that are all far away and spread out, not just in one place.

That’s why we see thousands of galaxies in every direction, not just in one spot near where the Big Bang happened!
